description: Plain-English definitions for every technical term in the questionnaire. Rendered as info popovers in the UI. Each entry: term, short definition, who it applies to, and an official or primary source.

hipaa.definition: A US law that protects health information (called PHI). Any cloud vendor that stores or processes PHI for you must sign a Business Associate Agreement (BAA) promising to protect it.
hipaa.applies: US healthcare providers, insurers and clearing-houses, and every company that handles patient data on their behalf.
hipaa.source_name: US Dept. of Health & Human Services (hhs.gov)

baa.definition: A contract under HIPAA in which a vendor promises to safeguard the health data you give it. Without a signed BAA you may not put PHI on that vendor.
baa.applies: Any vendor that touches US patient data for a HIPAA-covered organisation.

gdpr.definition: The EU's General Data Protection Regulation: rules on collecting, storing and transferring personal data, with consent, deletion and breach-notice duties. Transfers outside the EU need a legal basis.
gdpr.applies: Any organisation that offers goods or services to people in the EU or monitors them, wherever the organisation is based.

dpdp.definition: India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act: consent, purpose limits and breach notification for personal data of people in India. Cross-border transfer is allowed except to countries the government blocks. The DPDP Rules 2025, notified in November 2025, phase the duties in over 18 months.
dpdp.applies: Organisations that process digital personal data inside India, or outside India when offering goods or services to people in India.

pci_dss.definition: The Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard: security rules for anyone who stores, processes or transmits card numbers. Using a payment gateway's hosted checkout keeps most of your system out of scope.
pci_dss.applies: Every merchant and service provider that handles Visa, Mastercard, RuPay or other card data.

soc2.definition: An independent audit report on a vendor's security, availability and confidentiality controls. Enterprise customers often ask for one, and you need your vendors' reports to pass your own.
soc2.applies: B2B software companies whose customers ask for security evidence; not a law.

data_residency.definition: A rule that data must be stored in a particular country or region. It removes every vendor without a data centre there.
data_residency.applies: Regulated sectors, e.g. the payment data of Indian payment system providers (RBI 2018 circular) or contracts that require EU-only storage.

dau.definition: How many different people use the product on a typical day. StackSense uses it to estimate traffic and pick a scale tier.
dau.applies: Every product. For IoT, count active devices instead of people.

peak_rps.definition: The highest number of requests your servers receive in one second, usually at the busiest hour. Servers are sized for the peak, not the average.
peak_rps.applies: Every product with a backend. Leave it blank and StackSense estimates it from users and app type.

latency.definition: How long a request takes to answer. 'p95' means 95 out of 100 requests are at least this fast. Around 100 ms feels instant; around 1 s keeps the user's flow of thought.
latency.applies: Interactive apps, games, trading and anything a user waits on.

consistency.definition: Strong: every read sees the latest write, so balances and stock counts are always right. Eventual: different copies may disagree for a moment, which is fine for likes or feeds.
consistency.applies: Money, inventory and health records need strong consistency; social feeds and telemetry usually do not.

availability.definition: The share of time the service works. 99.9% allows about 43 minutes of downtime a month; each extra 9 cuts that by ten times and needs more redundancy and someone on call.
availability.applies: Every product; most new products are fine at 99.9%.

baas.definition: A hosted backend (e.g. Supabase, Firebase) that gives you database, login, file storage and realtime through an API, so you write little or no server code.
baas.applies: Small teams and MVPs that want to ship fast; less suited to complex domain logic or very large teams.

serverless.definition: You upload functions and the cloud runs them on demand, billing per request. No servers to manage, but functions can start slowly ('cold starts') and cannot hold long connections.
serverless.applies: Spiky or low traffic, event processing, teams that want zero server maintenance.

lock_in.definition: How hard it would be to move to another provider later. Proprietary APIs (e.g. DynamoDB, Firestore) mean a rewrite; open standards (PostgreSQL, containers) move easily.
lock_in.applies: Everyone; it matters most for long-lived products and hybrid or regulated deployments.
lock_in.source_name: Gregor Hohpe on martinfowler.com: Don't get locked up into avoiding lock-in

realtime.definition: The server pushes updates to the user instantly (chat messages, live cursors, scores) over a connection that stays open, usually a WebSocket.
realtime.applies: Chat, collaboration, multiplayer games, live tracking. 'Some' = notifications and live counters.

seo.definition: Making pages easy for Google to find and rank. Pages rendered as HTML on the server are indexed faster than pages built by JavaScript in the browser.
seo.applies: Content sites, shops and landing pages; not apps that sit behind a login.

offline.definition: The app keeps working without internet and syncs changes when the connection returns.
offline.applies: Field apps, rural users, mobile-first markets.

read_write.definition: Whether users mostly look at data (reads, e.g. a catalogue) or mostly create it (writes, e.g. sensor readings or chat). Writes are the harder part to scale.

data_shape.definition: How your data is organised: tables with relations, flexible documents, key-value pairs, time-stamped metrics, graphs of connections, analytics aggregates or vector embeddings for AI search.
data_shape.applies: Every product; most business apps are 'relational'.

vector.definition: Lists of numbers that represent the meaning of text or images, so you can search by similarity. Used for AI features like RAG (answering from your own documents).
vector.applies: AI search, chatbots over your documents, recommendations.

deployment.definition: Public cloud: rented servers and managed services. On-premises: your own data centre, so managed-only services are impossible. Hybrid: both, so everything must stay portable.
deployment.applies: Banks, government and hospitals often require on-premises or hybrid.

microservices.definition: A monolith is one deployable application; microservices split it into many small services that deploy separately. Microservices pay off only with several teams.
microservices.applies: Small teams should almost always start with a (modular) monolith.

mvp.definition: The first version real users can use. A short time to MVP favours tools the team already knows.

budget.definition: Monthly cloud spend only: hosting, database, bandwidth and managed services. Salaries and SaaS tools are not included.
budget.applies: Everyone. $0 means free tiers only, which some vendors forbid for commercial use.

cloud_preference.definition: AWS, Google Cloud or Azure accounts, credits or skills you already have. Used as a strong nudge, never a hard filter.
cloud_preference.applies: Teams with startup credits, an enterprise contract or certified engineers.

regions.definition: Where your users are. A server far from users adds round-trip delay (Singapore to Mumbai is about 60 ms).
regions.applies: Every product; choose 'Global' only if you really serve several continents.

data_volume.definition: Size of the main database, not counting images or videos (those live in cheaper object storage). A typical SaaS starts under 10 GB.
data_volume.applies: Every product; large volumes (TB+) favour analytics or horizontally scaling databases.

team_skills.definition: Languages and tools your engineers already know well. Familiar tools ship faster with fewer defects.
team_skills.applies: Every team; leave empty if you will hire for the stack.

platforms.definition: Where users run your product: in a web browser, or as an installed iOS or Android app.
platforms.applies: Choosing iOS/Android switches the frontend to a mobile toolkit (React Native, Flutter).

lsm.definition: A way a database stores data on disk: new writes go to memory and are flushed in sorted files that are merged later. Writes are very fast; reads may check several files.
lsm.applies: Write-heavy databases such as Cassandra, ScyllaDB and RocksDB.

olap.definition: Online analytical processing: queries that scan and add up millions of rows (totals, trends, reports) instead of reading or changing one record.
olap.applies: Dashboards and reports, served best by column stores such as ClickHouse.

oltp.definition: Online transaction processing: many small reads and writes of single records (an order, a login). This is what most app databases do.
oltp.applies: Shops, SaaS apps and banking ledgers on PostgreSQL or MySQL.

acid.definition: Four promises of a database transaction: it happens fully or not at all (atomic), keeps rules true (consistent), does not see half-finished work of others (isolated) and survives a crash (durable).

cap.definition: When the network between database copies breaks, a system must choose: answer with possibly stale data (stay available) or refuse until the copies agree (stay consistent).
cap.applies: Choosing between strongly consistent and eventually consistent stores.

lcp.definition: The time until the biggest visible element of a page, usually the main image or headline, is drawn. Google rates under 2.5 seconds as good.
lcp.applies: Web frontends where speed and search ranking matter.

multi_az.definition: Running copies of the service in two or more availability zones, which are separate data centres in one cloud region, so one building failing does not stop the app.

cdn.definition: A content delivery network keeps copies of your pages and files on servers around the world and serves each visitor from a nearby one, so your own servers see far fewer requests.
cdn.applies: Sites where many visitors see the same content.

sharding.definition: Splitting one large database into several smaller ones, each holding part of the rows (for example users A to M), so no single machine has to hold or serve everything.
sharding.applies: Databases beyond what one machine can handle.

connection_pooling.definition: Reusing a small set of open database connections instead of opening one per request. Databases handle only a few hundred connections, and serverless functions can open thousands.
connection_pooling.applies: Serverless backends on PostgreSQL or MySQL.

rpo_rto.definition: Recovery point objective: how much recent data you can afford to lose. Recovery time objective: how long you can be down before the service must be back.

edge.definition: Running code in many small locations close to users (for example Cloudflare Workers) instead of in one data centre, which cuts round-trip time but limits what the code can do.

orm.definition: Object-relational mapper: a library that lets code read and write database rows as ordinary objects, so you write less SQL by hand.
orm.applies: Backend frameworks such as Django, Rails and Spring.
